cim: Susceptibility Map-Weighted MRI Accurately Identifies Neurodegenerative
cim_eredeti: Susceptibility Map-Weighted MRI Accurately Identifies Neurodegenerative
szoveg_eredeti:
Susceptibility Map-Weighted MRI Accurately Identifies Neurodegenerative Parkinsonism With Artificial Intelligence Support

A diagnostic evaluation study has demonstrated that visual evaluation of susceptibility map-weighted magnetic resonance imaging can accurately distinguish neurodegenerative parkinsonism from non-neurodegenerative causes in patients presenting with clinically uncertain symptoms, with overall diagnostic accuracy and reader consistency increasing substantially when radiologists are assisted by artificial intelligence software. Differentiating disorders such as Parkinson’s disease from non-neurodegenerative mimics, including drug-induced parkinsonism, represents a persistent diagnostic challenge in routine neurological practice because clinical presentations often overlap. While dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography is established as an effective imaging modality to resolve such ambiguity by detecting presynaptic dopaminergic loss, magnetic resonance imaging provides a widely available alternative that could optimize the clinical workup if proven capable of resolving diagnostic uncertainty.

Parkinson’s disease is pathologically characterized by the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, which is accompanied by increased tissue iron accumulation specifically concentrated within the nigrosome-1 subregion. In conventional clinical workflows, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain has largely been confined to standard structural sequences intended to exclude secondary etiologies such as cerebrovascular disease rather than confirm neurodegeneration. To address this limitation, investigators focused on susceptibility map-weighted imaging, an advanced magnetic resonance technique that enhances susceptibility contrast by combining magnitude images with a quantitative susceptibility mapping weighting factor. Unlike conventional susceptibility-weighted imaging that pairs magnitude with phase information, quantitative susceptibility mapping yields voxel intensities that directly reflect magnetic susceptibility and correspond closely to local iron deposition. Consequently, susceptibility map-weighted imaging allows clear visualization of the healthy, cell-dense nigrosome-1, whereas neurodegeneration leads to loss of its visibility due to neuronal loss and iron accumulation.

To investigate the clinical utility of this sequence in an ambiguous patient population, researchers evaluated 180 consecutive adult participants presenting with parkinsonian syndromes whose treating neurologists could not confidently establish whether their condition was neurodegenerative after clinical examination and medical history review. Every participant had previously been referred for dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography between January 2019 and July 2023 across neurology outpatient clinics at the Amsterdam University Medical Center, Spaarne Gasthuis, and Flevoziekenhuis. The cohort comprised 120 men and 60 women with an overall mean age of 67.9 years, spanning an age range from 31.9 to 86.4 years. Across the entire cohort, 84 individuals received a final diagnosis of neurodegenerative parkinsonism, including 76 ultimately confirmed to have Parkinson’s disease, while 96 participants were determined to have non-neurodegenerative parkinsonism, including an unclassified subgroup that exhibited normal nuclear imaging without meeting defined diagnostic criteria for specific entities such as essential tremor.

Brain imaging was performed at Amsterdam University Medical Center on a dedicated 3-Tesla Ingenia system equipped with a 32-channel head coil. The imaging protocol utilized a three-dimensional T1-weighted MPRAGE sequence to guide the multiecho three-dimensional fast field echo susceptibility map-weighted imaging sequence. Technologists positioned the sequence in an oblique coronal-transverse plane perpendicular to the brainstem mesencephalon, spanning anatomical coverage from the posterior commissure down to the superior margin of the pons. Technical sequence parameters included an acquisition field of view of 192 by 192 by 32 cubic millimeters, a reconstructed acquisition matrix of 384 by 384, an isotropic in-plane spatial resolution yielding 0.5 by 0.5 by 1.0 cubic millimeter voxels, 32 acquired slices, a repetition time of 49.0 milliseconds, a initial echo time of 14 milliseconds with an echo spacing of 13.0 milliseconds across three collected echoes, a flip angle of 20 degrees, a receiver bandwidth of 100 Hertz per pixel, and an overall sequence acquisition time of 4 minutes and 55 seconds.

Four board-certified radiologists, whose experience in neuroradiology spanned between 8 and 30 years, assessed the reconstructed images independently while fully blinded to clinical histories, final clinical diagnoses, dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography scans, and other neuroimaging findings. Raters reviewed 20 training scans prior to study evaluation and subsequently graded nigrosome-1 integrity on axial reconstructions using a 5-point Likert scale designating structures as normal, likely normal, unclear, likely abnormal, or abnormal, alongside scoring scan quality as very poor, poor, sufficient, or good. After completing an initial unaided review of all study cases, the radiologists repeated the evaluation of the complete series with the assistance of commercial artificial intelligence software without an enforced washout period. The software package incorporated the Heuron IPD system, which automatically identified the anatomical position of the red nucleus to evaluate the adjacent inferior slices containing the substantia nigra using a convolutional neural network architecture based on YOLOX, and the Heuron NI module, which outlined nigrosome-1 and calculated volumetric metrics.

The study established its reference standard on the final clinical diagnosis recorded in electronic health records by attending neurologists during follow-up, which synthesized clinical course and dopaminergic imaging results. Dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography using iodine-123 fluoropropyl-carbomethoxy-iodotropane was acquired and interpreted under European Association of Nuclear Medicine practice guidelines, categorized as normal or abnormal through visual evaluation and local institutional specific binding ratios. Any inconclusive nuclear imaging cases were resolved by consensus between two blinded nuclear medicine specialists, while ambiguous neurological clinical categorizations were independently reviewed and adjudicated by two movement disorder specialists to achieve consensus. Extracted clinical questionnaire metrics revealed that the neurodegenerative and non-neurodegenerative groups presented with similar baseline motor impairment and cognitive profiles, as documented by Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale motor examinations, Beck Depression Inventory II scores, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores, though non-neurodegenerative cases recorded a slightly higher mean score on part I non-motor daily living experiences.

In the initial unaided visual evaluation, radiologists achieved a mean diagnostic accuracy of 79.5 percent against the reference standard, with individual reader performance ranging from 72.6 percent to 82.8 percent. Across all four raters, the mean diagnostic sensitivity was 87.8 percent, ranging between 70.7 percent and 97.6 percent, while mean specificity stood at 71.3 percent, with reader-specific values spanning from 47.6 percent to 87.9 percent. On average, the readers designated 8.3 percent of the scans as unclear, with rates ranging from 7.2 percent to 9.4 percent across readers.
